summary: Specifies a method for resolving IP addresses to HIPPI hardware addresses and for emulating IP broadcast in a logical IP subnet. It interoperates between HIPPI-800 and HIPPI-6400 equipment. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: HIPPI is an extremely fast network built for moving large amounts of data between computers. Its switches were not required to broadcast, and most did not, so a computer could not simply shout an address to ask who owns it. This document defines the replacement: a server that keeps a table of who is who, and answers address questions on behalf of the network, plus a way to make broadcast look as if it works.

questions: how does arp work over hippi
how is ip broadcast emulated on hippi
subtitle: How a very fast parallel network finds out which machine an IP address belongs to.

tldr.problem: HIPPI switches are not required to carry broadcast, and most did not. IP needs broadcast for several of its protocols and needs a way to turn an IP address into a hardware address, so both had to be solved for HIPPI.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines HARP, a variant of ARP and Inverse ARP that runs over HIPPI and uses a designated server to answer lookups when the network cannot broadcast. It also defines a broadcast emulation server that fakes IP broadcast on top of the HARP table.
tldr.outcome: This obsoletes RFC 1374 and, together with RFC 2067, defines address resolution for IP over HIPPI. It works with both HIPPI-800 and HIPPI-6400 equipment, and it was later updated by RFC 5494.

today: RFC 2834 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current definition of address resolution and broadcast emulation for IP over HIPPI. It obsoleted RFC 1374, and it was later updated by RFC 5494.

sections.title: What HIPPI Needs Address Resolution For
sections.content:
The ANSI High-Performance Parallel Interface is a dual simplex data channel. HIPPI can send and receive data simultaneously at 800 or 1600 megabits per second. Between 1987 and 1997 the ANSI working group standardized five documents that bear on the use of HIPPI as a network interface, covering the physical and electrical specification, the framing of a stream of bytes, the encapsulation of IEEE 802.2 LLC, the behaviour of a physical layer switch, and the physical-level and optical specification. The encapsulation document also implies the encapsulation of Internet Protocol.

HIPPI switches can be used to connect a variety of computers and peripheral equipment for many purposes, but the working group stopped short of describing their use as Local Area Networks. RFC 2067 describes the encapsulation of IP over HIPPI-800. This memo takes up where the working group and RFC 2067 left off and defines address resolution and LIS IP broadcast emulation for HIPPI-800 networks.

While investigating possible solutions for HARP it became evident that IP broadcast could easily be emulated for both HIPPI-800 and HIPPI-6400 hardware types. This is useful since HIPPI switches are not required to implement broadcast but many standard networking protocols rely on broadcast. The memo therefore further addresses the emulation of LIS IP broadcast as an extension of HARP.
sections.plainLanguage: HIPPI was built for speed, not for convenience. Its designers never said the switches had to forward a message to everyone at once, so most of them did not. Two things then had to be invented: a way to ask who owns an address without shouting, and a way to make broadcast work anyway.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of HIPPI Addressing
sections.content:
The document defines the terms it uses. A port is an entity consisting of one HIPPI source and destination dual simplex pair connected by parallel or serial HIPPI to a HIPPI-SC switch, which transmits and receives IP datagrams. A host is an entity, usually a computer system, that may have one or more HIPPI ports and which may serve as a client or a HARP server.

A switch address is a value used as the address of a port on a HIPPI-SC network. It is transmitted in the I-field, and HIPPI-SC switches map switch addresses to physical switch port numbers. A hardware address is the address of a port, consisting of an I-Field and an optional Universal LAN MAC Address. The Universal LAN MAC Address is a 48-bit globally unique address, administered by the IEEE, assigned to each port on an Ethernet, FDDI, 802 network or HIPPI-SC LAN.

HARP describes the whole set of HIPPI address resolution encodings and algorithms defined in the memo. It is a combination and adaptation of the Internet Address Resolution Protocol and Inverse ARP, and it also describes the HIPPI-specific version of ARP. Each host has a HARP table containing the IP to hardware address mapping of IP members. The HARP Request Address List is a list of ULAs to which HARP messages are sent when resolving names to addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Each HIPPI port has two names. One is its switch address, a short number the switch understands, and the other is a 48-bit address of the same kind that Ethernet uses. The table that maps IP addresses to these is called the HARP table.

sections.title: The HARP Request Address List
sections.content:
ARP was meant to work on the local cable, which gives it a local logical IP subnet scope. In the LIS scenario each separate administrative entity configures its hosts and routers within the LIS, and each LIS operates and communicates independently of other LIS's on the same HIPPI network. HARP has LIS scope only and serves all ports in the LIS, and communication to ports located outside the local LIS is usually provided via an IP router.

The requirement for IP members operating in a HIPPI LIS configuration is that all members of the LIS SHALL have the same IP network or subnet address and address mask. The document then identifies the HIPPI-specific parameters that must be implemented in each IP station connected to the HIPPI network.

The HIPPI hardware address of an individual IP port MUST contain the port's switch address. The address SHOULD also contain a non-zero ULA address, and if there is no ULA then that field MUST be zero.

The HARP Request Address List is an ordered list of two or more addresses identifying the address resolution services, and all HARP clients MUST be configured identically. The HRAL MUST contain at least two HIPPI hardware addresses identifying the individual HARP services that have authoritative responsibility for resolving HARP requests of all IP members located within the LIS. By default the first address MUST be the reserved address for broadcast, that is the address for IP traffic conventionally directed to the IEEE 802.1 broadcast address 0xFE1, whose ULA SHALL be FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF. It is REQUIRED that the second address be the address for messages pertaining to address resolution requests, 0xFE0, whose ULA is 00:00:00:00:00:00. The remaining entries are additional HARP server addresses, sorted in decreasing order of the 12-bit destination switch address portion of their I-Field.
sections.plainLanguage: Every machine on the subnet is given the same list of addresses to try when it needs help: first the broadcast address, then the official resolution server, then any others. Because every machine has the same list, they all agree on who is in charge.

sections.title: The Two Phases of HARP
sections.content:
HARP is a two phase protocol. The first phase is the registration phase and the second phase is the operational phase. In the registration phase the port detects if it is connected to broadcast hardware or not, and the InHARP protocol is used. In the case of non-broadcast capable hardware, the InHARP protocol registers and establishes a table entry with the server. The operational phase works much like conventional ARP with the exception of the message format.

Within the HIPPI LIS there SHALL be an authoritative HARP service, and at each point in time there is only one. To select it, each port sends an InHARP_REQUEST to the first address in its HRAL, the broadcast address 0x07000FE1 with the ULA FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF. If the port sees its own InHARP_REQUEST, then it is connected to a broadcast capable network, the rest of the HRAL is ignored, and the authoritative HARP service is the broadcast entry. If the port is connected to a non-broadcast capable network, then it sends the InHARP_REQUEST to all of the remaining entries in the HRAL, every address which sends an InHARP_REPLY is considered a responsive HARP server, and the authoritative HARP service SHALL be the HARP server which appears first in the HRAL.

The authoritative HARP server SHOULD be considered non-responsive when it has failed to reply to one or more registration requests by the client, to any two HARP_REQUESTs in the last 120 seconds, or if an external agent has detected failure of the authoritative HARP server. Should an authoritative HARP server become non-responsive, the registration process SHOULD be restarted. On a non-broadcast network the port is REQUIRED to keep registered with all HARP server addresses in the HRAL, and SHALL continue to retry each non-broadcast HARP server address at least once every 5 seconds until the termination criteria are met.

Once a HARP client has completed its registration phase it enters the operational phase, in which it SHALL gain and refresh its own HARP table by sending HARP_REQUESTs to the authoritative address and receiving HARP_REPLYs. A port is the target of an address resolution request if at least one of the following is true: the port's IP address is in the target protocol address field of the HARP message; the port's ULA, if non-zero, is in the ULA part of the target hardware address field; the port's switch address is in the target switch address field; or the port is a HARP server.
sections.plainLanguage: Two stages. First the machine asks whether the network can broadcast, by sending a request to the broadcast address and seeing whether it comes back to itself. If it does not, the machine registers itself with a named server instead. After that, lookups work like ordinary ARP, except that they go to that server rather than to the whole network.

sections.title: The HARP Message Formats
sections.content:
The HARP protocols use the HIPARP hardware type, protocol type and operation code data formats as the ARP and InARP protocols, and add an operation code for HARP_NAK. HARP messages SHALL be transmitted with the HIPARP hardware type code of 28, and SHALL be accepted if received with hardware type codes of either 28, 1 or 6. The hardware type SHALL contain 28 and the protocol type SHALL contain the IP protocol code 2048. The protocol address length SHALL contain 4. The requester's and target's hardware address lengths SHALL contain 10 if this is a HIPPI-800 hardware address, and 6 for HIPPI-6400.

The HIPPI message format for Internet datagrams conforms to the HIPPI-FP and HIPPI-LE standards, and the length of a HIPPI message, including trailing fill, shall be a multiple of eight bytes. The LLC value for SSAP-DSAP-CTL SHALL be 0xAA-AA-03 indicating the presence of a SNAP header, the OUI value for the Organization Code SHALL be 0x00-00-00 indicating that the following two bytes is an Ethertype, and the Ethertype SHALL be set to 2054, which is 0x0806. The total size of the LLC and SNAP header is fixed at 8 bytes.

For HIPPI-800 the hardware address is a 10-byte unit that SHALL contain the switch address AND the ULA. Two switch addresses are considered to be the same when they have the same 12-bit destination HIPPI logical address. In the case of HIPPI-6400 the hardware address is ONLY the 6-byte ULA, so the length of the hardware address clearly defines which version of HIPPI is being used. The use of ULAs is OPTIONAL but RECOMMENDED, and is REQUIRED if a port wishes to interoperate with a conventional network.
sections.plainLanguage: The message looks familiar if you know ARP: the same fields, the same idea. What changes is that the hardware address is longer, because a HIPPI port has both a switch address and a 48-bit address, and the length of that field is what tells the receiver which kind of HIPPI it is talking to.

sections.title: Emulating Broadcast with PIBES
sections.content:
HIPPI-SC does not require switches to support broadcast, and broadcast support has therefore been absent from many HIPPI networks. During its registration phase every port, including the HARP servers, discovers whether the underlying medium is capable of broadcast. Should this not be the case, then the HARP servers MUST emulate broadcast through an IP broadcast emulation server. A HIPPI IP broadcast server is an extension to the HARP server and only makes sense when the LIS does not inherently support broadcast. It allows common upper layer networking protocols such as RIP, TCP and UDP to access IP LIS broadcast.

To emulate broadcast within an LIS, a PIBES SHALL use the currently valid HARP table of the HARP server as a list of addresses called the target list. The broadcast server SHALL validate that all incoming messages have a source address which corresponds to an address in the target list. Only messages addressed to the IP LIS broadcast address, the multicast address or 255.255.255.255 are considered valid messages for broadcasting, and invalid messages MUST be dropped. All valid incoming messages shall be forwarded to all addresses in the target list. It is RECOMMENDED that the broadcast server run on the same port as the HARP server, and in that case the PIBES SHALL use the same address as the HARP server.

The document is explicit about the limits. A broadcast emulation service has an inherent performance limit: in an LIS with n ports, the upper bound on the bandwidth that such a service can broadcast is the total bandwidth divided by n plus 1, since each message must first enter the broadcast server and then be sent to all n ports. The server could forward the message destined to the port on which it runs internally, reducing n plus 1 to n. This service is adequate for the standard networking protocols such as RIP, OSPF and NIS, since they usually use a small fraction of the network bandwidth for broadcast, and it allows the HIPPI network to look similar to an Ethernet network to the higher layers. It cannot be used to broadcast high bandwidth traffic; for that, hardware support for true broadcast is required.
sections.plainLanguage: When the network cannot broadcast, the server pretends to. It keeps the list of who is present and sends each broadcast message to all of them one by one. That works for the small, infrequent announcements that routing protocols make, and it would not work for a video stream.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HARP messages are not authenticated, which is a potential flaw that could allow corrupt information to be introduced into the server system.

There are other known security issues relating to port impersonation via the address resolution protocols used in the Internet. No special security mechanisms have been added to the address resolution mechanism defined here for use with networks using HARP.

Not all of the security issues relating to ARP over HIPPI are clearly understood at this time. However, given the security hole ARP allows, other concerns are probably minor.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here is authenticated, so a machine on the network can claim to be somebody else. The document says so plainly and adds nothing to fix it, because the same weakness exists in ordinary ARP.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 1374
sections.content:
RFC 2067 obsoletes RFC 1374 but left ARP outside its scope because there was not enough implementation experience. This memo is an effort to clarify and expand the definition of ARP over HIPPI as found in RFC 1374, such that implementations will be more readily possible, especially considering forward interoperability with HIPPI-6400.

The changes from RFC 1374 are a new message format to acknowledge the HIPPI hardware address format and to eliminate the requirement of HIPPI-LE ARP for HARP to function; an explicit registration phase; additional message formats, namely InHARP requests and replies as well as HARP_NAKs; details about the IP subnetwork configuration; details about table aging; and IP broadcast emulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version of this protocol was never implemented, because nobody was sure how it should work. This version spells it out: the message format, the registration step, the extra messages, how the subnet is configured, how entries expire, and how broadcast is faked.

messages.label: INHARP_REQUEST
messages.note: Registration phase: the client announces itself and asks the server to answer for it.

messages.label: INHARP_REPLY
messages.note: The reply tells the client the protocol address by which the server can be reached.

messages.label: HARP_REQUEST
messages.note: Operational phase: the client asks for the hardware address of a target IP address.

messages.label: HARP_REPLY
messages.note: The reply carries the switch address and ULA that were wanted.

messages.label: HARP_NAK
messages.note: Sent instead when the requested address is not known.

items.label: HARP_REQUEST
items.desc: Asks for the hardware address of a target IP address.

items.label: HARP_REPLY
items.desc: Carries the hardware address that was asked for.

items.label: InHARP_REQUEST
items.desc: Asks for the IP address behind a hardware address.

items.label: InHARP_REPLY
items.desc: Carries the IP address that was asked for.

items.label: HARP_NAK
items.desc: Says that the requested address is not known. It is the request message copied with the operation code changed.

fields.name: Mode Byte
fields.desc: Extends the switch address to form an I-Field.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero in the address format as drawn.

fields.name: HIPPI logical address
fields.desc: The 12-bit HIPPI logical address defined in HIPPI-SC, held in the X and XX fields.

fields.name: ULA
fields.desc: The 48-bit Universal LAN MAC Address of the port. On HIPPI-6400 this is the whole hardware address, 6 bytes.

items.title: Target list
items.text: The broadcast server uses the current HARP table of the HARP server as its list of addresses to forward to.

items.title: Validation
items.text: Only messages from a source address on that list, and addressed to a broadcast or multicast address, are forwarded. Invalid messages are dropped.

items.title: Where it runs
items.text: It is RECOMMENDED that the broadcast server run on the same port as the HARP server.

items.title: Bandwidth limit
items.text: In a subnet with n ports the upper bound is the total bandwidth divided by n plus 1.
